utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. I hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Anna Richterova and Ann Sutherland for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman, with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, too. Any preliminaries? Just to inform you, our decision on the Rule 68 and other matters, other related matters, will be handed down later on today, hopefully before the registry closes. So I think we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are finished with this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very shortly, you will be starting with your evidence, with your testimony. And our rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be telling the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. In other words, you will be making a declaration which is the equivalent of an oath in those jurisdictions where an oath is administered. The solemn declaration is contained, the text is contained, in a piece of paper which the usher is going to hand to you, and my request to you is to take that declaration and read it out loud. That would be your commitment with this Tribunal that you will be telling us the truth and the whole truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So very shortly, I am going to explain to you what's going to happen. You are one of the witnesses that the Prosecution has summoned to give evidence in this trial against Radoslav Brdjanin. The procedure that will be followed is a very simple one. For some time, you will be asked questions by Ms. Sutherland for the Prosecution. I understand that you are already familiar with Ms. Sutherland. You have met her before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once the examination-in-chief series of questions by the Prosecutor is over, then it will be the turn of the Defence lawyers to cross-examine you, to put a set of questions to you. This is a right that the Defence enjoys because the law requires parity of arms. The law does not give more rights to the Prosecution or try to obstruct the accused in his proper defence. Once cross-examination is a right, then it follows that you have a duty, a responsibility, not to make any distinction between the two, between the Prosecutor and the Defence. Your obligation is a very straightforward one. You have a duty to answer each question wherever it is coming from, irrespective of whether it is being made by the Prosecutor or the Defence counsel, your duty is to answer that question as fully as possible and certainly as truthfully as you are in a position to do. Having said that, I now invite Ms. Sutherland to commence her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Kerim Mesanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of July, 1955.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified in the Kvocka trial otherwise known as the Omarska trial on the 11th and 12th of September, 2000. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And since you arrived in The Hague, you've had an opportunity to review that testimony by listening to audiotapes of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, pursuant to the agreement between the Prosecution and the Defence, the Prosecution seeks to have the transcript of Mr. Mesanovic's Omarska testimony and the exhibits submitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. I have three copies for the Judges and one for the registry here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how you want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is confused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not the first time and won't be the last. It was my understanding that these transcripts were to be provided to you well in advance of the testimony of the witness so you would have a chance to go through them before the witness came and testified. And it now makes it quite difficult to proceed because any cross-examination I had for this witness was based upon my belief that you would have already read the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not much, Mr. Ackerman. It's from 514025220, and then from 5228 until 5246. I understand that you won't be proceeding with your cross-examination before Ms. Sutherland finishes her direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which will not be today, as I understand it. So I can assure you that by tomorrow afternoon when we meet again, we would have read this. And your concerns about not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My concern is not so much with today, Your Honour. There are witnesses coming where the transcripts are huge, and you won't be able to read them overnight between direct and cross, it's my understanding that those should be provided to you well in advance of the witness, and I just hope that that will happen in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, and that will happen with every subsequent witness that we seek to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In good time, because don't forget Ms. Sutherland, that I in particular, in the next weeks, will be dealing with Mrdja, Nikolic, plus also all the other cases pending before Trial Chamber II where I am not pretrial Judge because I happen to be one of the permanent Judges in Trial Chamber II. So more or less every week it's one or two or three other cases that I have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the oversight. I thought Your Honours had the transcript before, and we would just be submitting one copy of the transcript as an exhibit today. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We didn't have this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's my fault that you haven't been provided with it before today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The important thing because this we can easily handle. This is not much. It's an hour's reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As Mr. Ackerman rightly says, there are some witnesses that have two or three transcripts so you need them well in advance in order to read them. May I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, as discussed with you, your testimony today will focus on matters outside your Omarska testimony except for one or two questions which I will ask you in order to clarify or expand upon a couple of matters which were contained in your testimony. I will also be asking you to look at a number of documents. So I turn now to Prijedor in 1992. Up until that time, you had lived in the town of Prijedor for nearly 30 years, that is from 1963 until 1992.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You lived in the centre of Prijedor both with your parents and then with your own family after you married?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You worked in the mobilisation department of the secretariat for the people's defence for thirteen years from 1979 until 1992?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where is the building of the secretariat for the people's defence? Where was it in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The building of the secretariat for the people's defence was in the Mose Pijade Street number 2, as part of the building of the secretariat for internal affairs. Later, in 1986 or 1987, an annex was built in the courtyard of the museum for the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned the secretariat for internal affairs, did that have an acronym?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was called SUP for short.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1128-2, please, the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, because the transcript says P118, exactly. So it should be 1128.2. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I don't think -- okay, it is being corrected now. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you just place it on the machine to your left. Using the pointer, would you point to where the secretariat for people's defence offices were.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Starting from this building in the -- on the ground floor, this is where a recruitment affairs were. This is where the reserve officers and labour duty affairs were located. Then this is the section for mobilisation affairs, and this one was just purely military duty. And this part here was the office where I was working on automatic data processing. You don't see from here the part that was added on some time in 1986 or 1987. This building was constructed later as part of the SUP. So it was all -- this is all here, the first, the second floor --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You are pointing to the right-hand side of the picture. For the people's -- secretariat for people's defence offices?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said your office --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- was the bottom left-hand corner office where the mobilisation office was?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, where I am pointing, that was the mobilisation part, and this is where I worked in this building here. This is the office where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many floors did the secretariat for people's defence occupy?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The addition had three floors including the ground floor, and then on the other side there were some parallel offices which belonged to the secretariat for the people's defence. In the middle there was a corridor. There were five offices facing the street, and there were five offices on the other side of the building looking on to the SUP courtyard. In this part there were three floors added on to the secretariat for people's defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And besides that area you just mentioned, the rest of the building was taken up by the SUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And another part back in the courtyard which consisted of federation for conferences, a car repair shop, a cell, a restaurant, and a room where the files were kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as you've discussed in your Omarska transcript, and we won't go back over it, the cell that you just referred to at the back of the SUP was where you were taken when you were arrested, was it not?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's in the courtyard of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with that photograph. Sir, what other buildings are in the immediate vicinity of this building, what other government buildings?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the photograph we just had, to the left, there was the court building. As I said, part of the secretariat for people's defence was built as an annex in the museum courtyard. So just in front of the building, the view we saw in the photograph, that was the old building of the municipal assembly of Prijedor and behind there was the administration building of the Ljubija iron ore mine that was behind the old municipal assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown this document, please. Your Honours, copies were distributed either Monday or Tuesday. And Ms. Gustin has informed me that the map should be marked as P1.1. Your Honour, do you want to give Mr. Mesanovic's Rule 92 bis testimony an exhibit number at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say P1.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: P1.1. P1, the town maps of Prijedor, and this document is based on those town maps that were marked by Mr. Inayat in his earlier testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that make sense to you, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, just looking at that -- looking at the photographs, are you able to tell the Court what they are photographs of?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I need to put my glasses on. Which number should I start with, or is it important?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Starting with number 1.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 1 is the building, the municipal building. Number 2 is the SUP building. Number 3 is the old town. To the right you can see the River Sana and the Prijedor Hotel. Number 4 is the Mladost sports hall, it was part of a technical school and gymnasium. Number 5 is Trnopolje. What I am pointing at, that is the Dom building, and then the shop, the school that my late father had worked in for almost 30 years. Number 9 is the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks. Number 8 is the youth district of Benkovac, in which I had spent part of my time before the war with different youth activities. Number 7 is Keraterm. I skipped number 6, that's Omarska. The Olakovic [phoen] Restaurant, the hangar, and the red house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned number 3 as Stari Grad. Was that a settlement of houses?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a settlement of an older type. According to as much as I can remember, and I can see here the Lovac Restaurant. It was owned by Kozara Turist. You can see it here below the old linden trees. It was on the way into the old town or as we refer to it, "K". That was a favorite place for excursions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of persons that lived in the Stari Grad area?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think 99 per cent Muslims. I even know a Serb lad who lived there, but he was married to a Muslim woman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in that photograph, you said you could see one building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's over here. It was called Lovac, hunter. It was a restaurant, and it was owned by the Kozara Turist company. That was a catering company in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that area of Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to accounts by my colleague, Haka Hodjilic [phoen] who lived in this part roughly, and he came there after the attack on Prijedor, they cleared up the old town with tanks starting with the mosque and then going around the town. I don't know if you know about this, but those were old houses mostly made of timber and earth. And that was a protected area. It was supposed to be renovated as a protected area, and it was supposed to remain the old town. That was before the war, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also mentioned number 8 as the youth district in Benkovac. Do you know whether there was a military installation at Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not before the war. It was envisaged as a youth district, and it was a Yugoslav federal level building operation, and there was a project and there was supposed to be six buildings in it representing each of the republic and then an essential building representing the federation. It was supposed to symbolise Yugoslavia. It was some sort of a youth district for sports and recreation activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, would it be fair to say that through working in the centre of town and privately, you came to know a lot of the citizens in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Most, yes. The great majority, especially people belonging to my generation or within five or ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1190 and also P1182. If the witness can be given P1190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, did you give him the document? Could you put the English version on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what is the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The 5th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is minutes of the second session of the National Defence Council of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Looking at the items on the agenda, what is agenda item 1?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Discussion of the decisions on mobilisation and the passing of resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then looking at conclusion number 2, could you read that conclusion, please.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The municipal secretariat for national defence is to reinforce the TO detachment and the war unit 4777 in conjunction with the military department and in accordance with the request made by the commanders of these units."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that was conclusion number 1. Since you've stated it, the TO detachment --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's okay. The TO detachment, did that have a war unit number?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was T-08949. That was how the detachment was numbered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know of a war unit numbered 8316?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the 5th Kozara Brigade, 8316. That's how we referred to it. But that was the 5th Kozara Brigade, the TO unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what is war unit 7777 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: At first, it was an infantry regiment. I don't know exactly until when. And then it was converted into a motorised brigade. It evolved into a motorised brigade, I think the 43rd Motorised Brigade. It evolved from a regiment into a brigade. I don't know exactly how long before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the JNA name for the war unit 4777?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think they called it the 43rd Motorised Brigade. I know that it was military post 3670 Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Have you heard of the 343rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite probably there was -- that was that because what I gave you was a three-digit number but mostly it was two-digit numbers. So perhaps we used to refer to it as 43rd so that's why I remember that. It refers to the former regiment and then became the motorised brigade 4777.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you read the conclusion numbered 2.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The mobilisation orders following from the decision of the autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina assembly are to be carried out when the actual situation and the municipality renders it necessary and in accordance with the needs and special plan through callup papers issued by the municipal secretariat for national defence."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you now look at Exhibit P1182. What is the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: 4th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who is the signature block on the document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The document apparently signed by Milorad Stakic, excuse me, Za -- in my copy, it's illegible. The last two letters I and C. I couldn't really tell which the third letter is. It's illegible. It's very difficult to see and quite illegible. Milorad Sahic [phoen]. Is it Sahic perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at the very top of the document, the block on the very top of the document, could you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, republic secretariat for national defence --" correction, "regional secretariat for national defence. Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sahic." I've never heard of this institution. That's not before the war, it never even existed, regional secretariat for national defence. Such an institution never existed before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you look at the decision numbered 1. Could you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "A call for general public mobilisation on the entire territory of AP Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then if you go back to P1190, and conclusion number 2, the mobilisation orders following from the decision of the autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina assembly are to be carried out, and it continues. Did you carry out this mobilisation until your arrest on the 24th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What ethnicity of persons were you mobilising?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: During this period, I was only mobilising people of Serb ethnicity, only people of Serb ethnicity. They were in the files and in the databases, they were there as Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with those two documents. Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you proceed with the next question on this new document, just to make this clear, the document that you have been referring to, the Serbo-Croat version, the third line from the top --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of P1182, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Can you read out the first word in the third line, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the top I said. From the very top. The third line in block letters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regional secretariat for the people's defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... translate it republic secretariat. Make a note of it, Ms. Sutherland, and then perhaps you can come back to us on it. Because it does make a difference, regional is regional and republic is republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, does your English version say at the top that it's a revised translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good fix, huh?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. While you have Exhibit P1190, which is the other document, who presided over the meeting of the National Defence Council on the 5th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Stakic, Dr. Milomir Stakic, president of the council for the people's defence presided over the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit P1268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I note in 1190, for example, there is a reference to municipal secretariat for national defence. Then it becomes republic secretariat for national defence. But it is indeed a regional secretariat for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour if --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Witness, can you look at Exhibit P1190. Conclusion number 2 talks about mobilisation orders from the decision of the autonomous region Bosanska Krajina assembly, and it is to be carried out through callup papers issued at the municipality level. Is that correct? And this municipal secretariat for the national defence is the department that you worked in in Prijedor in 1992, is it not?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that clear, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, just wanted to draw the distinction because he referred to in the beginning of his testimony today, he did refer to that, and then when he's referring to the regional secretariat for national defence, he made a categoric statement that this never existed before the war. So at some point in time, there must have happened something which either brought into the existence the regional secretariat for national defence. But it seems that the regional secretariat for national defence appears on a document dated 4/5/92 which predates by one day the document which is P1190. So we have a statement and a confirmation of what he had stated earlier, but still leaves the matter a little bit hazy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Witness, you weren't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, before you ask a question. Judge, I'm wondering, the other day we had an exhibit that the translation was wrong and the year was wrong. It was 1993 when it should have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And now today we have got this one. Does anybody undertake the responsibility to substitute a corrected translation into the exhibits in this case? Because if not, there are exhibits that we know are wrong and because we are sitting here we know it, but somebody looking at these exhibits in the future is not going to know that they are incorrect translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we will look into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So substitutions would be nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll look into it. My legal officer will remind me of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also think that we have on a number of occasions said that we were requesting revised translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And they are in the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Indeed you did. Indeed you did. Sorry for all these interruptions, Ms. Sutherland. I know that they are frustrating, but you see, what worries me is if you look at 1182, whoever translated it, at page 2 of the English version right at the bottom of the page, you have before the name Colonel Milorad Sahic secretary of the regional secretariat for NO. So why on earth he or she here translates the word into regional but translates the third line, the beginning of the paragraph, into republic just is beyond me. I can't understand it. Because the same word is translated into republic in one instance, and into regional in another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, looking at Exhibit P1268, if you can, in the -- if you can go to decision numbered 19 at the top, do you have that? It's a decision of the 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. "Pursuant to Article 110 of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina number --" I think, "32/92 and Article 4 on the decision of the organisation and operation of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality, number - something - /92, the Prijedor Municipal Assembly on its session of May 22nd, 1992, adopted the following decision and appointment to Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that at a meeting of the 22nd of May or the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In the English translation, Your Honour, it says 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's speaking of the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can see here is the 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That will have to be another revised translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did the Prijedor Municipal Assembly adopt? What was the decision?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "This decision is made for the president, the vice-president, and members of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality. The following people are appointed, one, Dr. Milomir Stakic, president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly is appointed president."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a need for him to read out the names of the members of the municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, do you know any of the people listed from 1 to 10 in this document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Milomir Stakic, when I say I know him, I don't know him personally. I know him as someone from the same town. Savanovic, Dragan as well. Dr. Milan Kovacevic, Slobodan Kuruzovic, Bosko Mandic. I don't know Bosko Mandic. I used to know Simo Drljaca. Slavko Budimir was a colleague of mine. Later, he became the secretary of the secretariat. Ratko Travar, I can't remember that man. Vojo Pavicic is a neighbour of mine, a childhood friend. We grew up together. Dr. Zeljko Macura, I know him personally. And Vojo Pavicic, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want you now to view a videotape, and tell me whether you recognise anyone on the videotape that is listed on the document or if there's other people that are on the videotape that are not listed on the document as well. If the audiovisual director could play video V000-0084 and if that could be marked for identification as P1129, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop us. When you want to point out any individual or anything in this videoclip, just say the word "stop," and the technicians will stop, will freeze the picture, and then you can tell us exactly what you want to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I apologise for the bad quality of the tape. It's the best we could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the purpose of playing the tape is for recognition of individuals, then I would suggest that the sound not be turned on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There is no sound on this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the town of Prijedor. Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you could rewind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, stop. Slavko Budimir, the secretary of the secretariat for people's defence. My former colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Using your pointer, can you -- no, I'm sorry. You can't. What gentleman are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about the man sitting at the head of the table and is looking at the screen on the right side, Slavko Budimir, the secretary of the secretariat for people's defence. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, because to me, there are two persons sitting more or less at the head of the table. One wearing a dark jacket, and the other one wearing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. He's wearing a jacket, and a white shirt, probably a white shirt. And he is sitting at the head of the table just like I am. The other person is in a jacket and he is bald. This other person that I am talking about has more hair and is wearing a jacket.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person on the right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The person --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The picture is fuzzy, but I think this is Simo Drljaca, this person here. Maybe if you can play it a little bit. I think he has a moustache. And then there is Dr. Kovacevic, if that's a moustache.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, you're pointing with the pointer to the computer, but we are not able to see that, what you are pointing at. The person that you referred to as Drljaca, what colour shirt is he wearing in the photograph and where is he sitting?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He is sitting in the left corner of the screen. He's bent over slightly, and he is wearing a white shirt. He is in the centre of the left corner. And then if this is a moustache, then that's Dr. Milan Kovacevic to the right. The man, is this my right-hand, to the right, there's a man with a wedding ring on his hand, and if you could play it a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Stop. This is Dr. Kovacevic. And could you please play it a little bit forward. His hand is a little bit in the way, but it looks like Dr. Macura. Stop. The person, I think he's holding a cigarette in a military uniform, so the first from the front of the screen, that's Major Radmilo Zeljaja. I don't know the military officer or person with glasses. Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can just say for the record, we're looking at 11.36.36.11.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: This is finally Dr. Kovacevic, the person that I said has a moustache. He's holding a cigarette in his left hand. Stop. In the right-hand corner of the screen on the right side of the screen is Simo Drljaca in the corner with a suit jacket and a white shirt. This is Dr. Kovacevic, and then this other person I don't see very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For the record, the video was paused at 11.36.48.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You are saying that Kovacevic is on the left and Drljaca is on the right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Drljaca is on the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If the video could be played again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop again. Radmilo Zeljaja again. I think that's him. I can see him better now. He's on the left side of the table. There are two persons sitting on each side of him. On one side is a person in a military uniform that I don't know. Can we continue please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 58.16.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. The person on the left side with his left-hand on his ear with a watch on his wrist is Slavko Budimir. So that's the man in the left side of the screen. Then there's a person on the right side who has his right hand on his shoulder. That's Dr. Zeljko Macura.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is stopped at 11.37.07.08. Could you play the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Stop. Could you stop the video, please. Completely stop. Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1218.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, this is a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality of a meeting held on the 22nd of May, 1992. And it's a decision about the mobilisation on the territory of the Prijedor Municipality. Could you read the first paragraph numbered 1.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "All conscripts assigned to the following war units, 4777, 3507, 5456, 6817, 2982, 3839, 6588, 4853, and TO 8316 are requested to immediately report to their war units. Those conscripts who are assigned to other war units than those mentioned above are obligated to report immediately to the military district Zarko Zgonjanin barracks in order to be given instructions with regard to the mobilisation."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to read the first paragraph to show the source of the authority of the decision. Since we went through that with another document just a few moments ago, just to be fair I think that should be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, could you please read the first paragraph at the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the decision of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the general public mobilisation of forces and materiel in the Republic, the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality, considering the current situation and conditions at the meeting held on the 22nd of May, 1992, reached decision about the mobilisation on the territory of the Prijedor Municipality."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the war units listed in paragraph numbered 1, you have mentioned in your testimony already today that war unit 4777 was the 43rd Motorised Brigade from Prijedor. You also said that --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- war unit TO 8316 was the 5th Kozara Brigade. Can you tell me --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- given your experience in mobilisation, can you tell me what war unit 3507 is?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise in my best -- I will do my best to explain because it has been ten years since that event. So I will try my best to explain. The 3507 was the Banja Luka rocket unit. This is what we called it amongst ourselves. Its place of mobilisation was in the village of Dragocaj near Banja Luka. We provided for a part of this unit. I don't remember the exact number, from the municipality of Prijedor, and we made up the numbers from military conscripts. I think this number was perhaps 200 to 300 conscripts, not more, and the rest of the manpower was filled by Banja Luka and Gradiska, and this is how these units were manned 100 per cent according to the demands -- regulations regarding war units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At the moment, I just wanted you to tell me what the name of the units were. So unit -- war unit 5456?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: 5456, if I remember, was a Partizan brigade. 6817 was the engineers's regiment. 2982 if I remember well was the 6th Partizan Brigade. 3839, I think, was also the same. It was one of the Partizan Brigades in the territory of Banja Luka. 6588 I think its place of mobilisation was in the Mali Logor barracks in Banja Luka. It was a smaller unit with mainly police specialties because in the Banja Luka area was mostly the military police and accompanying units. 4853 was a very interesting unit with long-range missiles and exclusive command over this unit was kept by the presidency of the SFRY. We would provide the reserves for this unit, and they were mostly people who had at least completed high school level of education. They were mostly engineers, math teachers, because there was a lot of calculation involved in the work of these units in the territory of Banja Luka. 7316 was I've already said was the Kozara Brigade, it was the TO Kozara Brigade in the area of Prijedor. And it was 100 per cent filled up by military conscripts from the town of Prijedor and the Municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in relation to 5356, the Partizan unit, and 6817 the military engineers, where were they based?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: 5456 was in the area of Banja Luka, and 6817 was also in Banja Luka, in the Banja Luka area, in the village of Bosanski Aleksandrovac. And there was another subunit which was part of the larger unit, and it had a numerical insignia. So at the Level 4 -- it was at the level of a company. The main unit was 6818. And the 6817 as we used to call, its mobilisation place was also in Aleksandrovac. But twice a year, it was mobilised for training at the Jasenovac bridge. This is a bridge which was over the River Sava. I attended these exercises on several occasions because the mining installation to mine the bridge was already installed, not only for that particular bridge but for other bridges as well in accordance with the National Defence doctrine in order to defend ourselves from the enemy from several directions. So twice a year, they would go to check the bridge installations and to undergo training.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, can I please ask you to speak a little bit more slowly so that the interpreters are able to keep up with you. You are speaking very quickly. You mentioned that the war unit 4853, the long-range missiles, was the exclusive command of the presidency of the SFRY. You're referring to the time pre-18 May 1992, are you not?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the period that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that a number of these war units were -- to report, you would have to go to Banja Luka. Why would people from Prijedor be mobilised in these, for example, Banja Luka engineers or rocket missile brigades?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: This would be a longer story. From the earlier system, the orders would come by military mail from the republican secretariat, through the military post.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, would you please pause there. The interpreters would like you to slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that I just asked you, is it the reason these people were mobilised in the two examples I gave you because they have specialised experience in those war units, what those war units are about?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly so, only because of their specialisation. Because Banja Luka did not have certain specialties, then we would go to nearby municipalities and wider. So we would request a certain number of specialties for the reserve officers who were subject to military conscription.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where would the majority of conscripts from Prijedor be earmarked to go? You said a moment ago that war unit 8316 would be 100 per cent Prijedor conscripts. Where would the majority of conscripts go from Prijedor, into what war unit besides 8316?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: To the 3507, 6817, 3832, 39, and 6588, these were the units which were not 100 per cent filled by the manpower in the town of Prijedor -- the municipality of Prijedor. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There seems to be a misunderstanding. My question was where would the majority of Prijedor conscripts be mobilised to? You mentioned two units a moment ago, 4777, which was the 43rd Brigade, and 8716.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The remaining number of the units were mobilised in the environs of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so from your answer, I gather that the majority of the conscripts would have been mobilised into 4777 and 4316 [sic]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with that document. Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1278.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just before that, let's correct this for the record. According to the transcript here, your question was: "And so, from your answer, I gather that the majority of the conscripts would have been mobilised into 4777 and 4316."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where we have "4316", it should be 8316. 8316.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. You don't need to apologise. It's not your fault anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, do you have P1278 in front of you? Sir, this is a document dated June 1992, the title being "The Instructions on the Establishment, Composition, and Tasks of the Local Crisis Staffs in the Prijedor Municipality."

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And at the top left-hand block, it reads "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not on my copy. We're talking about the same document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does it say "Srpska Republika Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Has the witness got P1278?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I can explain to you what's happening for sure. The first page of the Serbo-Croat version is on the back page, on the back of the last page -- all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yeah, it's under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to lodge an objection with regard to this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the B/C/S original of this, it appears that it's nothing more than a draft. The dates and things were not filled in in the first paragraph. There's no stamp on it. There's no signature on it. And the appearance of it is that it was never adopted or disseminated. It's just an unadopted -- unused draft. That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could well be --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it goes to the weight of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. It could well be it was never approved, but that doesn't mean to say that that excludes it from admissibility in evidence. It may still be important as a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it may change the way -- it may change the effect that it has, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. Definitely. But it doesn't mean to say the fact that there is nothing to show that this decision was ever taken means that the draft cannot be admitted in evidence, for whatever it may be worth. So please go ahead, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, can you look at paragraph number 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a bit. Did he answer the question that you had put?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Going back to the title on the top left-hand corner of the document, does that say "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can turn to paragraph number 11, could you read out that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The local Crisis Staffs are to carry out other work in accordance with the decisions and other documents passed by the Assembly, the Presidency, and Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, competent organs of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and the Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staffs."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's exactly the basis of the objection that I made. If this was never adopted, if it's just a draft that was discarded, then this paragraph is senseless, meaningless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's wait for the next question, Mr. Ackerman. We've had documents like this, and then the next question -- I mean, I wouldn't suggest the question, but I am anticipating what the next question is going to be. And I am that sure you are anticipating the same question. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, reading the paragraph that you have just read, do you know whether these -- the local Crisis Staffs carried out their work in accordance with what is stated in paragraph number 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just no way he could know that unless he was in each of the local Crisis Staffs and worked in each of the local Crisis Staffs. There's no foundation for that question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer it. Let him answer it. Can you answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew that they did carry it out because they received the military callups, according to the sectors that they covered. Callup papers, they would place them -- they would implement them in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you go to paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the interpreters have the document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The interpreters haven't got a copy of the document and they want the English translation put on the ELMO machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you -- is it on the ELMO? Yes, okay. Are the interpreters happy? Thank you. Yes, please start reading it again, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is talking about the previous paragraph, paragraph 12 talks about the composition of the local Crisis Staffs. What does paragraph 13 state?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The ex officio staff members are as follows: The military unit commander whose area of responsibility is the local territory [appointed as the president's assistant for military affairs] and police station or police unit commander in charge of the local territory [appointed as the president's assistant for security].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Whenever it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we will take a break now. Is it agreed we will only break for 15 minutes? The interpreters are happy with that? And the technicians?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the technician needs 20 minutes, for the relay of the other broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed. And please, slow down because I want to make sure that the interpreters don't tire themselves out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P1268. It was the Official Gazette of the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, can you please go to the decision numbered 34.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a decision from the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff issued from its meeting of the 7th of June, 1992, and the decision was on the demolition of structures war-damaged beyond repair. Under paragraph 1, it lists a number of streets in Prijedor. I think you would be better at pronouncing them than I. Could you name the two streets that are mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about Esad Midzica Street and Ivo Lola Ribara Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have in my hand a very large version of the town map of Prijedor. Smaller versions have been admitted as P1, and I have shown this to Mr. Ackerman yesterday. It's the only copy I have. If we could use this document because the names of the streets on P1.1 and P1.2 are illegible. So we need the big map in order for the witness to see the street names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we proceed along that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So we'll put that on the ELMO, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry about that. I suggest, Ms. Sutherland, first you indicate to the usher where you are going to direct the witness to so that he would place the appropriate part on the ELMO because otherwise, we will just get lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I hope this will be the right area. And if that could be marked P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need to mark it? Because if it's actually an enlargement of P1.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It can be an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. If it is -- I just stated that because that's the only copy you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we will have it admitted in evidence as Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, using the pointer, can you point to where Midzica Street is?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Serdmica [phoen] Street is parallel to Marsal Tito Street, which is the main street in the town of Prijedor. That's about here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just point to where the SUP building is on that map.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The SUP building is in this area here. Street number 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you move the document a little bit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then zoom in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then zoom in, exactly. Move it to the right, please. But I can't see now. Yes, and could we zoom in a little bit further for the time being. Yes, okay. So you are pointing at a spot where there is number 13? Or number 11, 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm pointing at number 10, that's the SUP building. This rectangle you can see here is the SUP building, behind number 10. And then behind number 10 is the annex building in the courtyard. Esad Midzica Street, this section here, the dotted line which is parallel to the main street, Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, what is number 11 on that map, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 11 is the building of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so the street that you just pointed to was just to the left of the Municipal Assembly building, the broken line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This broken line here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the majority -- what was the ethnicity of the majority of inhabitants of that street?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know, obviously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Starting with the back of the Balkan Hotel, in the back of the hotel, there was Alihrdjic Djuzin with his cafe and restaurant, and this is the Centar cafe which remained in that street. There was Henja who owned a kabob shop. This section here was Muslim -- all houses were Muslim. And in the centre there was the public building of the Kozara Turist company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't remember what the --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Ivo Lola Ribara Street is in front of the Municipal Assembly building. Also, that's this section here at the corner. We called it Jereza Mira Cikota Ulica, so it came out onto the house of Srdo Srdic, which was demolished by mistake or I don't know why at that time because there was an Albanian there owning business premises in the house. But aside from that, Simo [sic] Srdic, a person he took care of was living in the same house. He owned a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That was his stepson.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction. Srdo Srdic's stepson --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the majority of the residents in Ivo Lola Ribara Street, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Ivo Lola Ribara, there was Srdo Srdic's house, but there were Muslim houses too. I think it was the president of the SDS for a while. And I think his house disappeared from -- well he didn't exactly live there. He had rented a house to use for the restaurant. That sort of thing. And most of the street was inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, looking now at decision number 36 in the Official Gazette, in Exhibit Number P1268. There is Ivo Lola Ribara Street mentioned again. And that is also, I'm sorry, decision number 36 is a decision on the demolition of structures war-damaged beyond repair. And it's a decision emanating from the Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff at its meeting of the 9th of June, 1992. As I've just said, Ivo Ribara Street is mentioned. There is also another street. Mira Cikota Street. Can you point to that on the map, and can you tell me what ethnicity of persons lived in that street, the majority of people, if you know? Can you point to the street.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: This is Mira Cikota Street, so to the left and to the right from here, there was predominantly -- there were predominantly Muslim houses. To the left and to the right because there was a radio amateur association here. And then down the street from there, all the houses were Muslim as far as the street corner where the orthodox church was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You are pointing now to the right of Stari Grad. Can you show the Judges where Stari Grad is on the map?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, to the -- Stari Grad is this section here, this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you also point to Partizanska Street.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Partizanska Street runs parallel to the right river bank of the Sana River. So here you have Marsal Tito Street, and then it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can we zoom out.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you point to the street again.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It begins here at Marsal Tito Street, and then it heads off here. Here you have the Ljubija iron ore mine, part of their services. And then this road leads to the Celpak company. And then on the right river bank, and the right-hand side of the street, if I may call it that, at the entrance to the Prijedor Hotel, there was a Serb house below which there was a cafe and some business premises. And then you had a number of Muslim houses with a butcher's shop, and a bakery, and two or three cafes and restaurants. The entire right-hand side until the Obola Cafe, so all the houses in this part were demolished between the entrance to the new Prijedor Hotel as far as the Obola cafe on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There is also in the decision of the 9th of June 1992 Ilija Bursaca Street.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Ilija Bursaca. Just take a moment. Ilija Bursaca Street is here, number 23. The junction. So that's this street.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the majority of the residents of that street, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a mixed street. There were both Muslims and Serbs there. Here you have Radio Prijedor and Kozarski Vjesnik, the newspaper, at number 23. Just across the way is my uncle's house, and that house was demolished, too. The house next to it was a Serb house which was preserved. At the corner there was Hamdija Kurtovic's house, he was a panel beater, and his house had been torn down. Next to his was a Serb house that was whole and next to it was a Muslim house again and that house, too, had been demolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Also mentioned is Suljanovica Street. Can you point to that street on the map.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a street running parallel to the flow of the River Sana called Berek, and it led to the part of town called Skela with 90 per cent Muslim population. That's also the street that which leaves the junction of Pitolo Street here, and running almost parallel to this island called Stari Grad, and then it takes you to this section here. That's Hrumonovic Ulica. And then this part, just on the way in, that, too, was demolished. I think there was a mosque here, and I think the mosque also was demolished during the first attack. And on the way out towards the old Prijedor-Bosanski Novi Road, all the houses there were demolished because there was 90 per cent of Muslims there, there was some Catholics there, some Ukrainians, too, but predominantly Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The people who lived in Suljanovica Street, what was the ethnicity of the majority of the inhabitants in that street if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think almost a hundred per cent Muslim in that section.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, these two decisions issued on the 7th and 9th of June, 1992, respectively, are you aware of when the damage occurred to these streets that are mentioned in these two decisions?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll clarify it. These two decisions issued on the 7th and 9th of June, 1992, in relation to the war-damaged houses, in all of the streets mentioned in these two decisions, are you aware of when the damage occurred to the houses, the residences, in these streets, the buildings in these streets that are mentioned?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 30th or 31st of May. It was the end of May, and there were allegedly some operations. I have no idea, because I spent all that time in my house. These houses were subjected to combat operations. There was fire being opened on them by the enemy, so the houses were torn down. I think it was either on the 30th or on the 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you refer to "the enemy" who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the Muslims as opposed the Serbs who were tearing down the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Who do you say caused the damage to these Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian army or whatever they were called.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier, when you were shown Exhibit P1.1, which was the town map with the photographs around it, you pointed to one of the photographs being Stari Grad. And you said that "they came and cleared Stari Grad with tanks." Who are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian army came in with tanks. The story was told to me by a colleague of mine who had remained without any possessions. He could only keep what he was wearing the day he got out of the old town, Stari Grad. Here is where the junction was, and the mosque. The first thing they tore down was the mosque. And they stood on the plateau outside the mosque and the houses were old. So even a detonation could cause them to be destroyed. And then they just opened fire on whatever they could sight in front of their barrels.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P1237.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a -- what is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who is the document signed by? Or who is the signature block on the last page?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose this reads chief of the public security service. It says Rljaca, so presumably Drljaca, Simo Drljaca. That's the last thing I see, Rljaca, Drljaca, at least as far as I can see, Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And does the block at the top of the document on the first page on the left-hand side read "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, Security Services Centre Banja Luka, public security station Prijedor"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you please read paragraph -- the first paragraph after the date.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "With a view to the speedy and effective establishment of peace on the territory of Prijedor Municipality, and in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff, I hereby order the following:"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you read the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The industrial compound of the Omarska mine, strip mine, shall serve as a provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or detained on the grounds of the security services operational information."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that the place where you were detained from late June until early August 1992?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you turn to paragraph numbered 17. Who implemented -- who was responsible for implementing this order?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The implementation of this order shall be supervised by police chief Dusan Jankovic. Jankovic, Dusan. In collaboration with the Bana Luka security services centre and with the support of authorised executive personnel."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have finished with that document for the moment but if it could be kept at the witness table because I will refer to it in a moment. Could the witness be shown another document. This does not have a Prosecution Exhibit Number. It was closed as Document 4.2147. And if it could be given the next exhibit number which is P1130.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated the 23rd of June, 1992. The signature block is the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, Dusan Baltic. Who is the document addressed to?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: To Simo Drljaca, chief of the public security station Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you please read the first paragraph and the first conclusion, the first two conclusions, please.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The Prijedor municipality Crisis Staff has entrusted this service with the task of drafting a report on the implementation of the conclusions, orders, decisions, rulings, and conclusions adopted at its meetings. In order for this service to be able to develop the report it is requested for you to submit in writing information about the realisation of those Crisis Staff conclusions or whose implementations -- for whose implementations you or the station have been made responsible and which have been forwarded to you in a timely fashion, specifically conclusions number 02-11-108/92 dated 31st of May, 1992, and the following conclusion number 02-111-109/92." Shall I just read on?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does it say there those two conclusions are dated the 31st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you read what has been added by hand next to those two conclusions.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Forbidding the release of prisoners. Funds --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's sufficient. That's in relation to the next conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1282.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated the 1st of July, 1992. The signature block at the bottom of the document is chief, public security station, Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who is the document addressed to?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It's addressed to the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the reference is your documents numbered 02-111-236/92 dated 23rd June, 1992, and number 02-111-236/92 dated 30th of June, 1992. Could you please read the first sentence and the first conclusion.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "In reference to your documents of the above numbers and dates, we hereby inform you that: Conclusion number 02-111-108/92 by which the release of prisoners is prohibited is being fully observed." Excuse me, you said the second conclusion, too? Should I read out the second conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I said the first conclusion. Could you read the final conclusion? It's a decision just before the signature block.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "Decision of the Banja Luka Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff number 03-531/92 dated 22nd of June, 1992, on staffing executive posts and other posts important to the function of business establishments has been implemented in this public security station." SJB, I suppose that means public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1238. Your Honour, I have better copies of the B/C/S version, of the original, of this document. The copy that I had in my binder was cut off at the bottom. I don't know whether yours is as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ours is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is document -- yes. Its ERN number 00633780.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is -- what is the title block on the top left-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Municipality of Prijedor Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you read the first paragraph. "At its meeting held..." Could you read down to "Article 1."

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "At its meeting held on 2nd June, 1992, the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality adopted the following decision on the release of imprisoned persons: Article 1: All Serbs who have been imprisoned by mistake are hereby released from further imprisonment. Article 2: All soldiers and military personnel who have been imprisoned by mistake while actually on leave with the authorisation of the appropriate military authorities are hereby released from further imprisonment. Relatives of soldiers and policemen who have responded to the mobilisation callup and have participated in the war shall be released from further imprisonment on the basis of lists compiled by the military authorities and confirmed by the commanders' signature or on the basis of lists compiled by the police organs and confirmed by the signature of the chief of the public security station. All persons older than 60 for whom an investigation has been confirmed that they did not commit an offense are hereby released from further imprisonment. Other prisoners may be found --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you please slow down. Could you please slow down for the interpreters. Could you please read from Article 4, again.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
