utterances.text: "All persons older than 60 for whom an investigation has confirmed that they did not commit an offence are hereby released from further imprisonment. Article 5: Other prisoners who may be found not guilty in legal proceedings conducted by competent organs shall be released from further imprisonment. Article 6: The public security station shall be in charge of the implementation of this decision, and the chief of the public security station shall be deemed personally responsible for it, as he has the exclusive right to sign orders to release any imprisoned person." Signed, Crisis Staff. And I can't identify the stamp and the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Going back to Article 1 of the decision, "All Serbs who have been imprisoned by mistake are hereby released from further imprisonment." Do you see any reference to Muslims or non-Serbs who have been imprisoned by mistake, whether they are hereby released from further imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a problem deciding whether that's a question or a submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because we all know that it doesn't say that -- it's just a way for her to argue to you that it doesn't say it, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, I think let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, witness, please answer the question which was put to you. And the question stated precisely the following: "Going back to Article 1 of the decision, all Serbs who have been imprisoned by mistake are hereby released from further imprisonment, do you see any reference to Muslims or non-Serbs who have been imprisoned by mistake, whether they are released from further imprisonment," that is specifically in reference to Article 1, not with reference to any of the other articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't see anywhere that non-Serbs or Muslims are being released. Only Serbs are being released from further imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at Article 5, you were detained in Omarska from -- you were arrested on the 24th of June, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were taken to Omarska shortly thereafter where you stayed until the beginning of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you ever charged with any offence and legal proceedings were conducted?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown P1237 again, which should be on the witness table.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you read a moment ago paragraph numbered 1. Looking at the order establishing this "provisional collection centre," who was assigned the task of interrogating the detainees?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The inspectors were given this task, a team of -- a mixed team of inspectors who would come to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you please read paragraph 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "A mixed group consisting of national, public, and military security investigators shall be responsible for the work with and categorisation of detainees. They shall organise themselves respecting the parity principle, Mirko Jesic, Ranko Mijic, and Lieutenant Colonel Majstorovic shall be responsible for their work."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mirko Jesic, do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long have you known him for?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably the entire time that I worked at the secretariat, for that entire period, but actually he was a teacher by profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he have any other function before the war?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he worked in the State Security Service. That's what we called it. As an inspector of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his position within the State Security Service? You said he was an inspector. At what level --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the State Security Service, right up until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ranko Mijic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. My former friend, a friend of many years' standing, we spent a lot of time together. We even attended the same school for six months. He was the chief of the criminal investigation service. His nickname is Bajo, and most of the citizens of Prijedor know him as Bajo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you went to the same school together. Which school was this?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a school from the former system, a party school, a higher political school of the league of communists. He went on behalf of the SUP and I went on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often would you get together with Ranko Mijic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Almost every day we met at the SUP. We would have coffee at noon, or if our joint friend came, he was a drummer with Divlje Jagode, then we would go to a nearby cafe and have a drink. This was permitted under the old system.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Majstorovic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you know it was him? Were you told?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to what the other inmates said, he wasn't very tall. He always carried a brown briefcase in his hand. And every time that he came he would pass by the glass house, so I did see him. According to stories by the inmates, Halim Mesic, who often cooperated with him and who was in the same room as me, I heard from him that this was a Lieutenant-Colonel from Banja Luka. What the two of them did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Mirko Jesic and Ranko Mijic were both from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were both from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often did you see them in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Mijic Ranko, every day, every work day, their work day. So this meant from Monday to Saturday. And I saw Jesic Mirko, Mijic occasionally. And I don't know whether this was once a week or twice a week but that's when I would see him. Mijic, Ranko would come every day during work hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you were detained in the glass house.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were detained there for the majority of your time at the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Except for the first three days which I spent in the white house, but all the time other than that I was in the glass house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was Mijic's office, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He was upstairs, like all the other inspectors. There were no offices on the ground floor. So on the first floor of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where would you see Ranko Mijic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was able to see him most frequently, most of their visits to Omarska, they would pass through the kitchen, if the weather was nice. They would jump in through the restaurant window because the parapet was low. The windows were low and it was summertime. So they would jump in through the window or they would pass through the kitchen door and they would pass through the line in which we were waiting for our meals and they would pass along the entire length of the glass house in front of us. So I was able to see him on his way in and out every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his reaction when he saw you?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the most painful thing was that he didn't have any response or reaction at all. He seemed to look through me. It was a very bad feeling, a man that you knew practically up until yesterday, this wasn't a long time ago. This wasn't years ago, with whom up until the day before you socialised with, you visited each other's homes. He did not ask me with any part of himself, not with his ears, his eyes, his mouth, how I was -- how I was doing. And he was the one who was in charge of everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking again at paragraph 3, what is your understanding of the words "categorisation of detainees"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there was simply a kind of categorisation at the end of interrogation, and there were people who belonged to the first, second, or third categories. People were placed in these categories, and they decided in which category a person would be placed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "they," who are you referring to, the interrogators, or these three gentlemen, the three that are named in paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In all states and in all hierarchies, it's probably the chief who was the one to decide, along with the recommendations of his workers. So the chief is the one who decides whether it would be the first, second, or the third category and who would be placed in which category. These are quite major things, first, second, or third categories.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours what you understand to mean by each of these categories, so starting with category 1.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Category number 1, unfortunately, was the worst category because on the 2nd of July or in early July, I was in that category. They were unofficially called the "cooling list." So when Brk, the inmate -- the camp warden's driver told me that and he explained to me what that meant, it meant it would be those people who were going to be iced, [Realtime transcript read in error "Geneva Convention"] and it was as if he had saved me. The second category were the people who were supposed to survive, who were supposed to serve out their sins that were ascribed to them. The third category were people who were innocent, more innocent than the previous group. They were supposed to go home. This is what we heard from the guards, from the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, what sort of people, though, would be put into this category 1, this cold list, so to speak? What was the Serbs' categorisation for category number 1?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what was seen at Omarska, when it was all over, you could see who were those who disappeared. They were mostly people at leading or key functions, intellectuals, the intellectual sector of the Muslim society, wealthier people, as they described them people who were well off. People who were in combat -- people who were declared to have taken part in combat against them. That would be the first category.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What would be the people in the second category? What would they have done, to be put into that category?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The second category comprised people who obtained weapons, helped out financially, and so on. That would be the second category, those who were politically on the side of the SDA, who had declared themselves politically on the side of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I want to draw whoever's attention needs to be drawn to page 54 line 14. There's a major error there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 54, line 19. The words "Geneva Convention" somehow got in there. They don't belong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The court reporters will listen to the tape to fix that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also got the impression when he was saying with regard to category 1, mentioning leading persons having key functions, intellectuals -- intellectuals, Muslim wealthier people, did you mention lawyers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said intellectuals. I don't know how it was interpreted. The intellectual section, so people who were highly educated, doctors, engineers, lawyers, judges, directors. The leading people at that time in Prijedor, and they disappeared over the period of those few months.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the people that were put into category 3, what was the categorisation for that category?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what we found out at Omarska, these were people who were briefly interrogated or were not interrogated. They were not interesting for official processing. These were mostly people from the countryside who could not have done anything according to them. They were officially uninteresting for processing as far as they were concerned. So most often they were not even interrogated, or if they were, it was for a few minutes. What are you doing here? Most often it would be for the case to register that person again. These were people who according to what was said were supposed to go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But they stayed in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think you mentioned a moment ago you heard it was common knowledge among the prisoners that these three categories, and I think you said you heard it from other detainees and from the guards. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the fate of the people put into category 1, i.e., those who were classed as extremists? You mentioned the cold list a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Those people ended up with a beating or murder. I can't tell you the manner of it because if a person who saw someone being murdered was not able to tell anybody about it. So there were few who actually could clandestinely see somebody being killed, but there was no murder being committed openly. These people were taken in the direction of the red house, behind the red house there was the mine area. There were no streets. The bus stations weren't there. They ended up there, and it has been ten years now, and they still haven't turned up. So it's an assumption that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you turn to paragraph 6 of the document.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "Security services at the collection centre shall be provided by the Omarska Police Station with an adequate number of policemen who shall be present at the collection centre at all times and shall organise guard duty according to the on duty/on call/off duty principle."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And paragraph number 11.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The security services coordinators shall submit a report" and I can't see at what time. "On the preceding 24 hours to the chief of the Prijedor public security station daily or immediately when the circumstances allow no delay."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And these security services coordinators are the three gentlemen referred to in paragraph 3. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And paragraph number 12.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The chief of security shall do the same with regard to the operation of the security services and possible security problems."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can see from paragraphs 11 and 12 that these three coordinators, and the chief of security, is to report to the chief of the public security station on a daily basis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we saw from decision number 19 in Exhibit Number P1268, which was the Official Gazette of the Prijedor Municipality, the decision number 19 being a decision of the Crisis Staff of the 20th of May setting up the Crisis Staff and giving a list of its members, that Mr. Drljaca, the chief of the Prijedor Police Station, was a member of the Crisis Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your opinion, who, in the camp, was the most responsible for the killings and the beatings which occurred?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Ranko Mijic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned in your Omarska testimony that one night around a hundred people were killed. And this is at page 5195 of the testimony. Do you know where these people were from?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Those people came from the hills, from Brdo, from Brdo. I apologise. I'm trying to block these memories, but I think these were people from Brdo who came after the cleansing of Brdo. I think that's what they said, that they brought them and put them in the white house. And that night was the first night that we heard shooting, and Brdo is Hambarine, Rizvanovici, Biscani, and Jugovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think you said that this happened towards the end of July. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to add something. My work colleague, unfortunately, Muhamed Burazerovic, was taken to the white house that night. He was taken to the white house together with the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He is from Prijedor, and he is an employee of the secretariat of the people's defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, it was not "he was taken" but he was killed together with the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Halim Mesic, what was his fate, you mentioned his name earlier?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Halim Mesic spent most of the time with us in the glass house. I remember that a son was born to him. He was told that a son had been born to him at the end of June or the beginning of July and he wrote the date of birth on his jeans. He worked with professor Majstorovic. I don't know I wasn't really interested because nobody really talked much, we were afraid that the walls had ears. He was in the glass house all the time. After that, one night he was transferred by guards I don't remember them anymore, they wanted to kill him allegedly he was in the attack on Prijedor. He was their cousin. They took him to the white house and he did say once that they were not going to beat him but that they would have to kill him. But they beat him once. He survived that so that they would not beat him any more. And then it was that the guards were coming out of the white house. This was Halim. He was holding on to the door jam, and then someone said leave him, and then the shooting began, and he was killed in the very door. And if you looked at the white house, it was bullet riddled, and it was riddled when Halim was killed. That's when it was riddled with the bullets. He was not beaten. He died in the doorway of the white house, and he was killed by fire from an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very remiss of me. I should have showed you a photograph of the Omarska camp earlier. I am so familiar with this case it just goes without saying. Could the witness please be shown from the bundle of photographs the photograph marked with the ERN number 00409592.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, Ms. Sutherland, the witness was shown a photo of Omarska on Document P1.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's an aerial view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which we identified as number 6 -- photo number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's an aerial. This is a much closer photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is going to be 1128.4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the rear view model of Omarska. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, 9592. It should be the front view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not according to the index that I have. 9592 is the rear view. 9596 is the front view. Anyway, what I suggest is that you show the witness both photos, and then -- anyway, they speak for themselves. We can't really... As you say, it's probably right what you said. It's the index which is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you just show Their Honours the buildings, point with the pointer and name the buildings that are depicted in that photograph.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: This building here, this part of the building, that's the administrative building with the restaurant. This huge building is the hangar. And this small house here we refer to it as the red house because it was red. I think it was made of brick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Okay. All right now. Because I was just going to draw the attention of the technicians that we were watching the witness on the monitor but not what he was pointing at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, if you could, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the administration building with the restaurant. The hangar. Red house, that's what we called it. The red house because I think it was made of brick. And this here is the famous white house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this photo 9592 represents front view of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I think it's just the way -- if you look at it, if you were to approach the administration building from the back, then obviously that's the front view when you are looking towards the -- in the white house is in the distance. And I think that's how the index has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. There doesn't seem to be an entrance -- yes, there is an entrance in the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown the other photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, the main entrance is on this side here. This is the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, where is the main entrance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main entrance to the Pista area, and the main entrance to the building is this, what I am pointing at. I'm talking about the entrance to the administration building. There was a circular staircase. In the back, this is the back of the restaurant, the house, where the rubbish dump was. This is the entrance to the mess, and this is the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, the entrance to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown ERN number 00409597.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you point to the entrance to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. That's this area here. We used to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We used to -- circular stairs, yes. This is the main entrance to the ground floor, to the right. You go up to the first floor, and on the left you enter the restaurant. Here is the toilet. And then if you head straight, there's a corridor to the big dormitory that was used as a depository for the clothes of the miners working in the Omarksa ore mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This would be Document 1128.5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Mijic's office. Can you point in the direction of where that was. Interrogation rooms, where were they?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The interrogation rooms were on one of the floors, but I can't show you exactly where Mijic's was because I was only ever taken to the first one -- excuse me, the second door on the left. That was inspector Ratko Milosavljevic's room. And this room over here, that was Zeljko Meakic's room because I went to that room once, this office here. I think it was first -- the second on the right because I think the first on the right was a toilet door and then the second door on the right, that was Zeljko Meakic's office. He was the commander of the camp. And Ranko Mijic's office, I'm not sure where it was but it was somewhere on the first floor I think. I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, can you please slow down for the interpreters. Where were the interrogation rooms, on what floor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: On the first floor of the administration building. That's where the interrogation rooms were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we please go back to photograph P1128.4, the view of the whole camp. Can you point to where the glass house was situated.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: You can only see a small portion of it here as the open part. That's the glass house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the photographs for the moment. Mr. Mesanovic, I asked you a moment ago who you thought was most responsible for the killings and the beatings which occurred in the camp. Why do you say that? Sorry, you answered that Ranko Mijic was the most responsible. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Simply because after the inspectors left, lists were left behind to continue the work of the guards of the Omarska camp. In fact, those lists were left to Zeljko Meakic because he was the final executor of Mijic's daily errands, so he was the final executor of what Meakic would do during the day between 8 and 5 in the afternoon. Zeljko Meakic would then execute these chores, duties, afterwards, after 5.00 and until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened when these people -- what happened to these lists? What was done with these lists?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly what was done with the lists, but I knew that every time the guards would enter a room, as they didn't know, they didn't have any records available as to who was where. And then they would start from the first room with a piece of paper, and they would read out a name. Maybe there were many names on a paper. But they only had a slip of paper on which there was the first and last name of the guard who would be called out after the inspector left. And if that guard would return, we knew that maybe that was that. But if you suffered only a single beating, you wouldn't be in the first category. But those who never returned, we assumed that they would have been placed in the first category because they never came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall a number of people from Benkovac who were in the white house?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. On the 24th of June when I was brought to Omarska, I spent my first night in the white house. The second room on the right as you go in. There were 43 people inside, plus the 8 of us who had just arrived. That's 58 persons all together. I recognise Bahrija Foric, a young man from Kamicani. My father worked as a teacher in Kamicani, so I had known that lad from when I was -- we were both very young. He had been badly beaten. And he was the only one who was allowed to lie down because his kidneys had been broken. The 43 of them and two women, I know of two women for sure, there was Sadeta Medunjanin, and they left -- were set for an exchange in the direction of Bihac. So 43 men and two women. I can't remember the last name of the other one, but the name of the first woman was Sadeta Medunjanin. Because that day when they were taken away, the local barber did one of those women's hair. And then one of the women's husband was my secretary and the other's son lived in the white house and all she said was, "maybe my nana will come out at some point." I am headed for an exchange now, but we'll get back together at some point later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was the person, the name of the secretary you worked for? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becir Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his son's name?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: One of his sons was killed in Kozara. I don't know his name. And the one who survived, his name is Anes Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned in your Omarska testimony a visit to the camp by international journalists, and this is at page 5198. And you were shown three stills from a video. And they are exhibits now attached to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to play a short video of the meeting between the international journalists and some persons from the Serb authorities. And I wanted to ask the witness whether he could identify any of the people that met with the international journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. In the meantime, could you give us a number for the transcripts of the witness's testimony in the Omarska case, Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: P1131. Your Honour, I did ask earlier in the proceedings, but we moved on. So I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So P1131. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the video be played, that's V000-1402, without the sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, could you look at this videotape, and tell me whether you recognise any of the gentlemen on the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if this would be marked for identification as P1132.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, stop. Yes. This person here turned away, that his Simo Drljaca, and this person here is Milomir Stakic. Can you just rewind a bit because I think I recognised another person. No, no. There's only Simo Drljaca and Milomir Stakic. Simo Drljaca to the left with a man in a red T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a man called Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What does he look like?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe -- it's not a very polite way to describe him, but he's running bald and he's plumpy. At least he was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he was to the -- there is a person with a pink top on. The next person standing --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The man greeting the person in the pink T-shirt is Simo Drljaca. That's the man standing next to the man wearing glasses. The man wearing white and glasses, that's not Simo Drljaca. But the face, you can see to the right is the man with the glasses, and to the left is Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the man to the right --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: To the right, on the right shoulder of the man wearing the white T-shirt, so that's the man with the glasses wearing the white T-shirt, so just behind his right shoulder we can see Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If the video can be played.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Here you get a much clearer image. This is Dr. Kovacevic, Milomir Stakic, Simo Drljaca. I think that's Nada Balaban over there. But I'm not sure. She was a teacher of English but I can't be sure really. At the head of the table, she has her right hand on her -- left hand on her chin, but her hand is covering her face now so I can't see her clearly. If you can just rewind a bit. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can play the video through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue, please. No, no the one pointing the finger, that's Milomir Stakic. The man smoking next to him is Dr. Kovacevic. Yes, yes, it's clear now. That's professor Nada Balaban, she is a teacher of English. I know this lad, his face is familiar but I can't remember his name. I knew him well. It's just that I can't remember his name. This military officer here, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pause there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're saying it's Dr. Stakic on the left --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sitting next to Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, next to Dr. Kovacevic, that's right. And then in the upper right corner of the screen, I see Nada Balaban, she is a teacher of English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we play the video again. And can we pause it at 2.47.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Or fast forward to 2.47.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simo Drljaca is back to his place at the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we keep playing the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Drljaca is sitting to --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: To the right of Mrs. Balaban. He just put his hands on the table now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pause there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first man in the upper right corner, that's Simo Drljaca. Just below the ICTY sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And could the video be played further on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the foreign journalists are at the top of the video. Could the video be stopped. Thank you. Could the next video be played, and that is without the sound as well. And that is V000-0401. And if that could be marked for identification as P1133. If it could be forwarded to 1.53.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Omarska. That's the entrance to the restaurant. On the left, there is the glass house, and on the right-hand side there was a toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Continue playing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still the restaurant. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The journalist from Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mean you don't know the person who was carrying the automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think his name was Drazenko or something like that. But he was in charge of the restaurant from the outside. But as the journalists were here, he came, in and then this journalist, I can't see him clearly, the bearded one, that's Rade Mutic, Radio Prijedor journalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The one with the camera gear or something in his hand? If the video can be played --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Military uniform, beard, and a camera, I think. I have no idea really. I think that must be a camera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never eaten this, at least not there. That was for this particular day. And you never ate at the table. You just get the food quickly and one eighth of bread and you would be sent running out. And I might be somewhere here. Stop. Can you just rewind a bit, please. This is outside the glass house. That's the corridor outside the glass house. Stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's looking into the glass house where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: From the restaurant looking from the restaurant into the glass house. Forward, please. Stop. This part here, around this column, because this is the end, left of here is the end of the glass house. I was the fifth from the wall to the right as we're looking. I see this should be Serif Kadic. And then next to him is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, this is -- these details of who is in the glass house and where they are sitting is in your Omarska testimony, so we will not go through that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, that is at page 5198 and following. Could the video please be played.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the way out from the restaurant, the exit. Stop. This is Simo Drljaca and Nada Balaban in the chief's office. Either Mijic's office or Zeljko Meakic's office. You can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the video please be played.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simo Drljaca. Nada Balaban, teacher of English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the video could be fast forwarded to when they are outside the camp. Stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Krkan. That's the main entrance, the stairway up there. And then these are people running back from the restaurant back to the hangar. And these other people are waiting for them to come out so that they could run into the restaurant in groups of 30, and then this is Krkan again. This is Nada Balaban, Simo Drljaca. I don't know these other two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Actually, could you please rewind the tape to the start of this conversation. And if the sound could be turned on. "SPEAKER: It, too, was under heavy guard. And we asked to be allowed to look inside. But in spite of promises of openness from the Serb-Bosnian leader Dr. Karadzic we were told we could see no more. "SPEAKER: Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us? "SPEAKER: He promised us something else, and said you can do this and this. And that, and not that. "SPEAKER: Our armed escort made it clear --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pause there, and turn the volume off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, stop. The man to the right wearing glasses, and his left hand braced, that's Zeljko Meakic. And to his left is Simo Drljaca with a Heckler gun in his hand. I don't know the man in the white shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If the video could be played again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And stop. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P1320.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I was going to suggest, but I need feedback from the interpreters in particular. If we could stop for about 5 to 10 minutes, giving the technicians the opportunity to change the tape, and then proceed and stop at 6.00. In other words, we will break for about 5 to 10 minutes now, and then we'll have about a quarter of an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One of the booths want a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15-minute break, then we have to stop. 15 minutes. How much more time do we have left? We won't resume afterwards. I mean at 6.00, we finish. In other words --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's fine. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we stop for about 5 to 10 minutes. And we'll resume from that. Because 15 minutes would leave us 5 minutes then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you interpreters, thank you technicians, and thank you, of course, everyone else. Let's proceed. We have a good 15 minutes, and then we'll bring it to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just before we play the video, I want to go back to one thing to clear up what may be a mistranslation or it may have been what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You talked about -- you told the Court today that you believe that interrogators would categorise the detainees into three categories. You also told us that many of those were placed into the first category. And those people would be killed. After Ranko Mijic and the other inspectors were responsible for making these decisions or making the lists, who actually carried out the killings? You stated that Meakic was the final executor of Mijic's work. What did you mean by final executor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The executor was Zeljko Meakic. He's the one who executed all of the orders.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the very last part of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, the interpreter didn't fully hear your last -- the sentence of your last answer. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The end executor of everything that the inspectors did in the course of the day was Zeljko Meakic. I said whether this was the first, second, or third category, depends -- the first category ended in murder; the second category most often ended in a beating or possibly with the backup of someone from outside of the camp, money had to be brought in in order to save his life. They had to provide a sum of 10.000 German marks or something. These were wealthier people. So it was some kind of financial assistance. Mostly we're talking about money. The third category was not touched and was not interrogated. The main executor after Ranko Mijic was Zeljko Meakic. He was the ultimate one. He placed a stamp on everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say executor, do you mean executioner or executor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that he was the one who directly said it. There were people who were subordinated to him. He would issue further instructions, notes for murder, beating, or for money because the notes came from the top. They didn't come from me. They came from the chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who would carry out these killings and beatings?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The end executor, the ones who did the task in a concrete way, were the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we please have the video played, V000-0401, continuing from after the Omarska camp. Sorry, if you could just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, after you left the Omarska camp in early August, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was brought to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think in your Omarska transcript, you said that you stayed there for approximately one day. And then you left the Trnopolje camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we please play the videotape, without the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This is Trnopolje. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is still Trnopolje. This is still Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this excerpt is about three minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is still Trnopolje. Stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you pause there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This is the Dom, the Dom, the cultural hall in Trnopolje. And this part here, excuse me, I apologise. The small building on the right side in the background behind the people who were standing at the wire fence is the old part of the school. That's where the shop was. And in this part here, in the very corner, there's a basket net, hoop. And this is where my father had his classroom. And it's an irony that I spent the night after 20 years in the same store where I used to come as a child to see my father. This was a sports hall, and the culture hall. In the small part, there were classrooms, and the teachers' apartments. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The small building you pointed to had a red, orangy coloured roof. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a black and white image. I didn't have one in colour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This is -- this young man is Fikret. I don't know his last name. I know he was with me at Omarska. This is on our arrival to Trnopolje. The first group was released before us, before we were released. A couple of days before Omarska was closed, and then some were taken to Trnopolje. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is still Trnopolje. Stop. We called this person "Kobas." He's a medical technician. We called him one wing, Krlac. He had only one arm. He would come to Omarska frequently with Dr. Ivic. But not to treat people. I don't know why they came. They were just in passing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This is -- this man who just came in behind this man with one arm, this is Dr. Idriz. I don't know his last name. He was at Trnopolje already. When I came there, he was with the vet, Azra, Azra Strikovic. This is Dr. Idriz. There was another doctor with him. Dr. Mensur Kusuran, who was moved to Kozarac, and he was moved to Trnopolje in July. He's the only doctor who survived from Omarska. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is still Dr. Idriz who, in the forefront of the image, he was in charge of Trnopolje. I think this is the sports hall, the gymnasium in Trnopolje. But I'm not sure. Stop. In the new school in Trnopolje. Stop. This is the SUP building in Prijedor. I don't know who the people are who are standing in front of it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This window here, I apologise, the first, second, third, fourth, the fifth window from the left to the right is the window of the office where I used to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the video can be stopped, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just to finish up with Trnopolje, before we break for today, when you arrived at Trnopolje, was there a fence? Was the camp fenced in any way?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at Trnopolje, we were simply unloaded across the road from the house where the Red Cross was. So we were taken inside behind the wire fence where there were two school benches and there were two inmates who were taking our names down. They were inside, behind the wire fence. We went out on to the street. We went into the -- through the main entrance. Inside, there were two desks, and there were two workers, two inmates representing the Red Cross because they were the ones who took our names down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, if you want to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You have been most cooperative, Ms. Sutherland. I thank you. So we will leave it at that for today. We resume tomorrow. How much time left you reckon?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I revised the exhibits, and I intend showing the witness ten documents which we will get through very quickly, and then there's one other document which doesn't have an exhibit number which has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So tomorrow, you will start the cross-examination pretty early I would imagine, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would think so. May I mention one thing very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was talking with the Registrar just a moment ago about this problem. For some reason Defence counsel are not on the distribution for the calendar that is updated every week so we never know for sure what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I don't know why that happens, but I thought we were sitting Monday I thought we were sitting in the afternoon. I found out at the last minute we had been moved to the morning. Because the schedule I had said afternoon. The schedule I have says we're not sitting on Friday but I heard a rumour yesterday that we are, so I don't know. We make plans based on the schedule we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I fully understand. I will try and find out if we could find a remedy for this. I don't know what the practice is frankly. I mean, I've never taken an interest to find out exactly who was on the distribution list and who isn't. You know, usually when I get something, it shows a long list, and I always ask why do we have this long list. But I never went through the list myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think you have considerable influence here, Your Honour. I think you could probably get us added to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the situation as it is now, today is the 30th. Today is the 30th. Tomorrow we are sitting in the afternoon. Right? In Courtroom III. Then Friday, the idea is to sit if necessary, if there is no objection forthcoming. But we have allotted Courtroom III, allocated Courtroom III for us if we sit on Friday. In the morning. And that would in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be because on the later schedule I know I received on the 18th of October, that's the latest schedule I am aware of, it had this Friday to be confirmed. We were always trying to catch up days. Obviously Mr. Ackerman didn't have a copy of that schedule so he didn't know this date is to be confirmed on Friday. Hopefully with the witness tomorrow, we will certainly finish Mr. Mesanovic, with the next witness, she is going to be another Rule 92 bis and some limited questions, and I don't know that Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination would take a long time. So hopefully we are going to be able to finish her tomorrow so we wouldn't have to sit on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we could do that, it would be better. I leave it in your hands. Perhaps you could take five minutes tomorrow morning or now after the session and sort it out. To us, it doesn't really make a difference. We'll try to accommodate both of you as much as we could. Have a nice evening. See you tomorrow afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 6.03 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 31st day of October, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
